Types of Holes and CNC Hole Machining Explained In CNC machining, few operations challenge process control and tool stability as much as blind hole machining. A blind hole is a hole that terminates at a defined internal depth rather than breaking through the opposite surface. Because the cavity is enclosed at the bottom, chip evacuation, thermal behavior, tool wear, and dimensional accuracy become far more difficult to manage compared to through-hole machining. These constraints make blind holes indispensable yet technically demanding features across precision mechanical parts, sealed housings, consumer products, and structural components. When projects require consistently accurate blind hole drilling, tapping, or fine-tolerance cavity machining, J LCCNC provides reliable depth control , specialized tool paths, and clean internal finishes, supporting both prototypes and full production. What Is a Blind Hole? (Quora) A blind hole is defined by its closed end. Unlike a through hole, which passes entirely through a workpiece, a blind hole stops before reaching the opposite side. The bottom shape varies depending on the tool used: conventional drills produce conical bottoms, whereas flat-bottom drills and end mills generate planar surfaces suitable for precision assemblies or tapping. The engineering purpose of blind holes extends well beyond simply preventing penetration. In structural parts, maintaining a continuous opposite surface preserves rigidity, prevents stress risers, and helps sustain load paths. In pressurized or sealed systems—pneumatic housings, pump bodies, battery enclosures—blind holes prevent leakage of fluids or gases. In aesthetic or ergonomic products, they allow components to be fastened internally without exposing screw holes on the exterior. Blind holes essentially balance internal functionality with external appearance, mechanical strength, and environmental protection. Blind Hole vs Through Hole Through holes are straightforward to machine because chips naturally exit, tools experience less thermal stress, and depth accuracy is less sensitive. Blind holes demand precise programming—typically down to fractions of a millimeter—because any error may result in breakthrough. Through holes favor higher cutting speeds and simpler setups, whereas blind holes influence manufacturing costs due to slower feeds, peck cycles, coolant optimization, and bottom-clearance requirements. This difference in machining complexity explains why blind hole features often drive DFM (Design for Manufacturability) considerations. Types of Holes in CNC Machining Hole geometry in CNC machining reflects functional intent. Through holes support fasteners, shafts, dowel pins, and alignment features, making them ideal for high-speed fabrication. Countersunk holes allow screws to sit flush with the surface, maintaining flatness in precision mechanical surfaces. Counterbores accommodate socket-cap screws and create controlled seating planes for load-bearing joints. Within this landscape, blind holes occupy a specialized category. They enable internal threads, hidden fastening points, or mounting cavities that must not disturb the profile or sealing plane of the component. In industrial machinery, blind holes allow assembly without compromising fluid channels or structural ribs. In consumer electronics, they maintain the clean, uninterrupted outer surfaces expected from modern design. The choice between blind and through holes ultimately depends on the balance between manufacturability and functional necessity. Blind Hole Machining Explained (Science Direct) Blind hole machining is more complex than ordinary drilling because the tool must operate inside a confined cavity with no path for chips to escape. As the flutes fill with chips, heat rises sharply and causes accelerated tool wear or material hardening, especially in stainless steel and titanium. This is why blind hole drilling strategies emphasize controlled chip load, coolant access, and stable tool geometry. Drilling Blind Holes Standard twist drills are used for most metals, but they form a conical bottom that may not meet design requirements. When engineers need a flat-bottomed blind hole—for example, to optimize the thread engagement length or to improve seating conditions—a flat-bottom drill or end mill is applied. Peck drilling cycles become essential in deeper holes, where periodic retraction clears chips and reduces heat. In high-precision applications, depth is repeatedly verified using machine probing or tool setters to ensure no risk of breakthrough. Depth Control and Tool Selection Depth accuracy is one of the defining challenges in blind hole machining. CNC tools rely on tool length offsets, spindle probing, or laser measurement systems to maintain consistency. Carbide drills offer superior rigidity for deeper holes, while coatings such as TiAlN or AlTiN stabilize cutting edges under heat. The selected tool often reflects not only the material but also the hole’s final function—threaded, reamed, or used as a locating feature. Material Behavior in Blind Hole Drilling Aluminum machines easily but forms long, continuous chips that can clog a blind cavity unless chip-breaking geometries are used. Stainless steel hardens quickly under heat and demands strict lubrication control. Titanium concentrates heat at the cutting edge, often requiring through-tool coolant systems. Engineering plastics behave differently—they may melt or smear if spindle speeds are excessive. The interaction between tool, material, and confined cavity defines the entire machining strategy for blind holes. Blind Hole Tapping (Blind Hole Tap) (Science Direct) Blind hole tapping is one of the most technically sensitive procedures in CNC machining. Unlike through-hole tapping, where excess chips simply exit the opposite side, blind hole tapping traps chips at the bottom. If unmanaged, these chips compact and cause tap breakage. Bottoming Taps for Blind Holes A blind hole tap—usually a bottoming tap—features very little chamfer, enabling threads to form almost to the bottom of the cavity. This is crucial when the full thread depth is needed for load-bearing joints, especially in aerospace or automotive parts. Plug taps and taper taps have longer chamfers and are not suitable for holes where thread engagement must begin close to the bottom. Best Practices for Tapping Blind Holes Effective blind hole tapping relies on rigid tapping cycles, stable lubrication, and precise pilot hole sizing. In difficult materials, spiral-flute taps help extract chips upward, preventing compaction at the bottom of the hole. Thread milling is often chosen when the material is prone to chip welding or when the design requires extremely tight tolerance control. The entire process must anticipate torque spikes, potential chip packing, and sensitivity to tool wear. Designing Blind Holes for CNC Manufacturing Blind hole design affects machinability more than most engineers initially assume. Hole depth must align with available drill and tap geometries, ensuring that tools do not deflect excessively. The bottom clearance should reflect the type of threading operation planned, and thin walls around the hole must be avoided to prevent distortion during machining. Depth, Diameter, and Tolerance The ratio between hole depth and diameter heavily influences tool stability. Excessively deep blind holes increase the likelihood of tool vibration, poor chip evacuation, and dimensional variation. Tolerance selection must reflect not only fit and function but also the realities of machining inside a confined space. Surface finish is another consideration: smoother walls reduce thread friction, improve fastener performance, and reduce wear during repeated assembly cycles. FAQ What is the purpose of a blind hole? To enable internal mounting, threading, or functional cavities without penetrating the opposite surface, preserving structure, sealing integrity, or aesthetics. Why is blind hole machining more complex than through holes? Restricted chip flow, higher heat concentration, and tighter depth accuracy requirements. How are blind holes tapped successfully? With bottoming taps, rigid cycles, proper lubrication, and chip evacuation strategies such as spiral flutes or thread milling. What is blind hole drilling? A controlled-depth drilling process designed to terminate precisely before breakthrough. Verify Now Blog > PCBWay Store NewArrival Product - M5StackChan AI Desktop Robot PCBWay Store NewArrival Product - M5StackChan AI Desktop Robot by: PCBWay Sep 24,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCBWay Store Link： AI Desktop Robot StackChan is a super kawaii AI desktop robot co-created by M5Stack and the user community. It uses the M5Stack flagship IoT development kit CoreS3 as its main controller, powered by an ESP32-S3 SoC featuring a 240 MHz dual-core processor, with 16MB Flash and 8MB PSRAM onboard, and supporting Wi-Fi and BLE. The main unit also integrates a 2.0-inch capacitive touch display with a high-strength glass cover, a 0.3 MP camera, a proximity & ambient light sensor, a 9-axis IMU (accelerometer + gyroscope + magnetometer), a microSD card slot, a 1W speaker, dual microphones, and power/reset buttons. The robot body, connected to the main unit, includes a USB-C interface for power and data, a 550 mAh battery, two feedback servos (360-degree continuous rotation on the horizontal axis and 90-degree movement on the vertical axis), two rows totaling 12 RGB LEDs, infrared transmitter and receiver, a three-zone touch panel, and a full-featured NFC module. The factory firmware is feature-rich, including an AI Agent, lively and expressive animations, ESP-NOW wireless remote control, and online app downloads. It can connect to a mobile app for video viewing, remote avatar control, and more, and also supports online updates (OTA). The product also supports programming via Arduino, UiFlow2, and other methods, and can connect to various expansion units in the M5Stack ecosystem, making it easy to implement a wide range of custom functions. Note: Includes 1 x Carrying bag or box (depending on the purchased product bundle) 1 x StackChan unit (with CoreS3 pre-installed) 1 x 50cm USB-A to USB-C Cable 1 x Character expression sticker 1 x Printed user manual Learn and Documents → DOCUMENTS Features Based on the CoreS3 main unit For detailed information, please refer to the CoreS3 page Robot body USB-C interface for power and data 550 mAh battery Two feedback servos (360-degree continuous rotation on the horizontal axis and 90-degree movement on the vertical axis) Two rows totaling 12 RGB LEDs Infrared transmitter and receiver Top-mounted three-zone touch panel Full-featured NFC Development platforms UiFlow2 Arduino IDE PlatformIO ESP-IDF Application Scenarios Desktop companion AI agent Voice-based question and answer Smart home IoT control Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > PCBWay Store NewArrival Product - M5Stack NanoC6 Dev Kit PCBWay Store NewArrival Product - M5Stack NanoC6 Dev Kit by: PCBWay Sep 30,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCBWay Store Wireless IoT Link： NanoC6 NanoC6 is a micro and low-power IoT development board in the M5Stack development kit series. It is equipped with an ESP32-C6FH4 SoC, supporting wireless communication technologies such as Wi-Fi 6 and ZigBee, and features a built-in infrared transmitter for convenient control of infrared IoT devices. The onboard ceramic antenna ensures a stable wireless communication connection. Additionally, the device is equipped with programmable RGB LEDs, allowing for personalized visual effects in projects. The inclusion of a Grove interface enables flexible expansion with various M5 devices (customizable to connect different types of devices, such as those following UART/I2C communication protocols), providing developers with rich hardware expansion possibilities. This development board is suitable for smart homes, industrial automation, health monitoring, and IoT devices, offering a comprehensive development solution for innovative projects. WiFi 6 M5NanoC6 is the first core control board to support WiFi 6, supporting the 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi 6 protocol (802.11ax) and backward compatibility with 802.11 b/g/n. WiFi 6 offers higher speeds, greater capacity, lower latency, and enhanced security compared to previous WiFi protocols. Verify Now Blog > How Vias Affect Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design How Vias Affect Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design by: Mila Sep 28,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout signal integrity high-speed PCB design via stub Anyone involved in high-speed PCB design has probably heard this rule of thumb: minimize vias in high-speed routing whenever possible. But many engineers know they should do this without fully understanding why. Some consider a via simply a “wire” and assume a few extra vias will not matter. Others believe that as long as the impedance is controlled, everything will be fine. It is often only after the board comes back for testing—with a collapsed eye diagram, increased bit errors, or EMC test failures—that they realize those seemingly insignificant vias may be part of the problem. A PCB via is one of the structures in a high-speed link that can introduce impedance discontinuities and parasitic effects. It introduces parasitic capacitance, parasitic inductance, via stubs, and changes in the return-current path. As signal edges become faster, these effects become increasingly important to signal integrity. 1. What Parasitic Parameters Does a PCB Via Introduce? Many engineers think of a via as simply a “vertical wire.” At high frequencies, however, a PCB via is actually a three-dimensional interconnect structure with parasitic capacitance, parasitic inductance, and transmission-line effects. Parasitic Capacitance (C_via) Parasitic capacitance forms between the via pad and the surrounding reference plane, such as a ground or power plane. Its value depends on factors including the via pad, anti-pad, distance to the reference plane, and dielectric material. T: Length of the via passing through the reference plane D₁: Via pad diameter D₂: Anti-pad diameter εr: Relative dielectric constant In typical structures, via parasitic capacitance is usually on the order of several hundred femtofarads (fF). Parasitic capacitance lowers the local impedance around the via and, together with other parasitic parameters, creates an impedance discontinuity that can cause signal reflections. Parasitic Inductance (L_via) The copper barrel and the vertical current path of a via also introduce parasitic inductance. h: Via length in the vertical direction d: Via diameter For a typical 1.6 mm PCB with common via dimensions, the parasitic inductance can be around the 1 nH range. Parasitic inductance increases the local impedance around the via and interacts with parasitic capacitance to affect high-speed signals. If the return path is not properly controlled during layer transitions, the additional loop inductance can also increase EMI radiation. Combined Effects of Capacitance and Inductance The actual electrical behavior of a via is not determined by capacitance or inductance alone. Multiple parasitic effects work together. By properly optimizing via dimensions, pads, and anti-pads, the impedance discontinuity can be reduced to some extent. However, when a relatively long via stub is present, the frequency response of the via structure can still exhibit significant resonance. 2. Why Is Via Stub a Major Concern? （Through Via and Via Stub） This is one of the easily overlooked issues in high-speed PCB design. When a signal travels through a through-hole via from the top layer to an inner layer, such as from the Top Layer to L3, the unused portion of the plated hole extending from L3 to the bottom layer L10 becomes a via stub. The Physical Nature of a Via Stub A via stub is essentially an open-ended transmission-line section. At certain frequencies, it can produce a significant resonance. The resonant frequency can be approximately expressed as: c: Speed of light (3×10⁸ m/s) L_stub: Via stub length εr: Relative dielectric constant When the via stub's resonant frequency enters the main frequency range of the signal, it can cause a pronounced notch in insertion loss. This can result in signal attenuation and waveform distortion and, in severe cases, lead to eye-diagram closure. Therefore, for high-speed signals, via stub length can be more important than considering the parasitic capacitance and inductance of the via alone. 3. Why Does a PCB Via Cause Impedance Discontinuity? （Via Impedance Discontinuities and Reflections） The impedance of a via, Z_via, is usually not exactly the same as the characteristic impedance of the transmission line, Z₀. For example, a common target impedance for a high-speed single-ended signal is 50 Ω. When a signal transitions from a transmission line into a via structure with a different impedance, part of the signal is reflected. The reflection coefficient can be expressed as: Γ = (Z_via - Z₀) / (Z_via + Z₀) If Z_via = 40 Ω and Z₀ = 50 Ω, then Γ ≈ -0.11. If Z_via = 30 Ω, then Γ ≈ -0.25. This shows that a larger impedance mismatch between the via and transmission line generally results in stronger local reflections. For this reason, via optimization in high-speed PCB design is not simply about avoiding vias. The goal is to minimize the impedance discontinuity between the via structure and the transmission line. 4. Why Should You Consider the Return Path During Layer Transitions? （Layer Transition and Return Current Path） A via can affect not only the signal itself but also its return-current path. When a signal changes layers, its reference plane may also change. For example, a signal may transition between routing layers associated with different reference planes. If there is no suitable return path near the layer transition, the return current may be forced to take a longer route, creating a larger current loop. This can lead to: Increased loop inductance Increased EMI radiation Degraded signal integrity Increased crosstalk Therefore, high-speed via design needs to consider not only how the signal travels, but also how its return current flows back. 5. When Do Vias Significantly Affect High-Speed Signals? Many engineers have the same question: if the parasitic parameters of a via are so small, can a via really affect a high-speed signal? When evaluating the impact of a PCB via, data rate alone is not enough. Signal rise time, via propagation delay, and via stub resonance also need to be considered. Rise Time vs. Via Propagation Delay The propagation delay of a via can be approximately expressed as: For a typical via with L = 1.2 nH and C = 0.4 pF: This time scale is usually relatively small. Therefore, for many common high-speed digital signals, the impact of the via's lumped L/C parameters alone may not be as significant as the resonance caused by a long via stub. However, as signal edges become faster, via geometry, impedance discontinuity, and return-path design become increasingly important to signal integrity. Via Stub Resonance vs. Signal Spectrum Instead of using data rate alone as the criterion, it is more important to consider whether the via stub resonance falls within the main frequency range of the signal. When these frequencies become close, the via stub can create a significant notch in the frequency response, affecting insertion loss, waveform quality, and eye diagrams. Therefore, there is no single data-rate threshold that determines whether a via will cause problems. The actual design should consider data rate, rise time, via stub length, Nyquist frequency, and channel loss together. 6. Why Is a Via a Weak Point in a High-Speed Link? A PCB trace can be designed as a relatively continuous transmission structure by controlling parameters such as trace width, dielectric thickness, and copper thickness. A via, however, has to perform a three-dimensional transition over a very short distance. As a result, a single PCB via may introduce: Parasitic capacitance Parasitic inductance Impedance discontinuity Via stub resonance Return-path discontinuity The trace is like a “highway,” while the via is more like a combination of a “toll station + sharp turn + dead-end road.” A single via may not cause a significant problem by itself. However, when multiple discontinuities appear along the same high-speed link, their effects can accumulate and eventually appear as increased insertion loss, return loss, or eye-diagram degradation. 7. How Can You Reduce the Impact of Vias? Minimize Unnecessary Vias High-speed signals should avoid unnecessary layer transitions and multiple vias within a short routing distance. During BGA fanout, optimize the component placement and routing-layer strategy to minimize the number of layer transitions for critical high-speed signals. Use Back Drilling For high-speed SerDes links and other applications with demanding signal integrity requirements, if the via stub enters the effective frequency range of the signal, back drilling can be used to remove most of the unused plated barrel. The primary purpose of back drilling is to shorten the via stub and reduce the impact of via stub resonance on high-speed signals. The required back-drilling depth and remaining stub length should be determined based on the PCB stackup, signal characteristics, and manufacturing capabilities rather than a fixed data-rate threshold. Optimize Via Anti-Pads The anti-pad affects the parasitic capacitance between the via and the reference plane. Anti-pad too small: Higher parasitic capacitance, which may reduce the local impedance. Anti-pad too large: Although it can reduce some parasitic capacitance, it may also create a larger opening in the reference plane and affect the return path. Therefore, via anti-pad dimensions should be optimized based on via size, stackup, reference-plane spacing, and target impedance, rather than using a fixed dimension. Add Ground Return Vias During a high-speed layer transition, ground vias can be placed near the signal via to provide a shorter, lower-inductance return-current path. For differential signals, the ground vias should also be arranged as symmetrically as practical to avoid significant differences in the return environment of the two traces. Optimize Via Dimensions Within the limits of manufacturing capability, via diameter, pad size, and via length can be optimized to reduce parasitic effects. For example: A smaller drill diameter can reduce some parasitic effects. A smaller pad can reduce coupling to the reference plane. A shorter via can reduce parasitic inductance and via stub length. However, smaller is not always better. Very small vias can increase PCB manufacturing difficulty and cost. Choose an Appropriate Stackup High-speed signal layers should be placed close to continuous reference planes to maintain strong coupling between the signal and its return path. For high-density, high-speed designs, blind vias, buried vias, and HDI structures can also be used to shorten the via length and reduce the impact of through-hole via stubs. Conclusion A via is not simply a “vertical wire.” In high-speed PCB design , it is a complex three-dimensional interconnect structure involving parasitic capacitance, parasitic inductance, impedance discontinuity, via stub resonance, and return-path changes. In many cases, the lumped parasitic parameters of a single via are not the dominant source of signal degradation. However, when a via creates a significant impedance discontinuity or its via stub resonance enters the effective frequency range of the signal, it can have a noticeable impact on insertion loss, waveform quality, and eye diagrams. Therefore, the key question in high-speed PCB design is not simply whether a via can be used, but: Will this via structure introduce an unacceptable discontinuity within the effective frequency range of the target signal? Minimizing unnecessary vias, controlling via stub length, using back drilling or HDI structures when appropriate, and maintaining a continuous return path are all effective ways to improve signal integrity in high-speed links. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing by: Mila Sep 16,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout design schematic design pcb layout services pcb layout design services PCB layout design is the process of transforming an electrical schematic into a complete, manufacturable printed circuit board (PCB). A well-designed PCB layout must do more than simply connect components. It needs to balance electrical performance, signal integrity, power integrity, thermal management, mechanical constraints, manufacturability, and reliability. For complex electronic products, decisions made during PCB layout can have a significant impact on product performance, production yield, cost, and time to market. A professional PCB layout workflow therefore requires systematic planning, engineering review, design verification, and manufacturing preparation. Below is an overview of the PCB layout design process we follow, from the initial schematic review to final manufacturing data.You can also find more information on our PCB Layout page . Step 1 – Design Preparation and Engineering Review The PCB layout process begins with a detailed review of the design requirements and source files. Before starting the layout, our engineers review the schematic and project specifications to make sure the design is ready for PCB implementation. This includes checking: Schematic completeness and connectivity Component information and footprints Board dimensions and mechanical constraints Layer count and stack-up requirements Component placement restrictions High-speed and differential signals Power distribution requirements Impedance-control requirements Thermal considerations Manufacturing capabilities and design rules If the customer only provides a PDF or image-based schematic, we can recreate the schematic in professional EDA software before proceeding with PCB layout. If the original schematic file is available, we can directly import the design data, generate the netlist, and establish the PCB design environment. At this stage, we also identify potential design issues that could affect layout, manufacturing, or product performance. Resolving these issues early helps reduce design iterations later in the process. Step 2 – PCB Stack-Up and Design Rule Setup Before component placement and routing, the PCB layer structure and key design rules need to be established. For multilayer and high-speed PCBs, the stack-up directly affects signal integrity, impedance control, power integrity, EMI performance, and manufacturability. Depending on the application, we may define: Number of PCB layers Core and prepreg materials Copper thickness Dielectric thickness Controlled impedance requirements Power and ground reference planes Minimum trace width and spacing Via structures and drill sizes Manufacturing constraints For high-speed designs, impedance-controlled traces and their reference planes are considered from the beginning rather than being treated as an afterthought. The design rules are then configured in the EDA software to ensure that the layout remains consistent with both the electrical requirements and the PCB manufacturer's manufacturing capabilities. Step 3 – Component Placement Component placement is one of the most important stages of PCB layout because it establishes the physical structure of the entire board. The placement strategy typically starts with components whose locations are constrained by the mechanical design, such as: Connectors Switches and buttons Mounting holes Displays Mechanical interfaces Heat sinks and other thermal components Core components such as MCUs, CPUs, FPGAs, memory devices, power ICs, and communication ICs are then positioned according to signal flow, functional relationships, and electrical requirements. Supporting components are placed close to their corresponding devices to minimize unnecessary routing length and improve electrical performance. During placement, we consider several factors simultaneously: Signal Integrity High-speed interfaces and sensitive signals require appropriate component relationships and short, well-controlled routing paths. Power Integrity Decoupling capacitors should be positioned close to the relevant power pins, while power distribution paths should be kept short and low impedance. Thermal Management Heat-generating components need sufficient copper area, thermal vias, airflow consideration, and appropriate spacing from temperature-sensitive devices. EMI/EMC Performance Sensitive analog circuits, high-speed digital circuits, switching power supplies, and other potential noise sources need to be appropriately positioned to reduce interference. Manufacturability Component spacing, assembly orientation, soldering requirements, and accessibility for inspection and rework are also considered. A well-planned placement makes subsequent routing more efficient while improving the overall reliability and manufacturability of the PCB. Step 4 – PCB Routing Once the component placement is finalized, the next stage is PCB routing. Routing is not simply about finding a path between two pads. The routing strategy must consider electrical performance, signal integrity, power distribution, EMI/EMC, and manufacturing constraints. Depending on the design, routing priorities may include: High-Speed and Critical Signals High-speed interfaces such as USB, DDR, PCIe, Ethernet, HDMI, LVDS, and other differential interfaces may require: Controlled impedance Differential-pair routing Length matching Skew control Appropriate reference planes Minimized discontinuities Careful via transitions Critical signals are routed according to their electrical requirements rather than simply following the shortest available path. Power and Ground Power distribution networks are designed to provide stable and low-impedance power delivery. Ground planes are carefully maintained to provide appropriate return paths and reduce unwanted noise and electromagnetic interference. General Signals After critical nets have been addressed, general signal routing is completed according to the defined design rules for: Trace width Trace spacing Via size Clearance Routing layers Manufacturing limitations For dense boards, routing may require multiple iterations of placement and routing optimization to achieve a balance between electrical performance and manufacturability. Step 5– Layout Optimization and Verification After routing is completed, the PCB layout undergoes a detailed optimization and verification process. This stage may include: Copper Pour and Plane Optimization Copper pours and power/ground planes are optimized to improve current return paths, grounding, shielding, and thermal performance. Silkscreen Optimization Reference designators, polarity markings, pin-1 indicators, and other assembly information are adjusted to improve readability and prevent interference with pads or other components. Design Rule Check (DRC) Automated DRC is performed to identify potential violations such as: Clearance violations Trace width violations Unconnected nets Via and drill violations Component spacing issues Copper-to-board-edge violations Other manufacturer-specific rule violations Engineer Review Beyond automated DRC, the layout is also reviewed from an engineering perspective. Depending on the project, this may include checking: Signal integrity Power integrity Thermal performance EMI/EMC considerations High-speed routing Manufacturing constraints Assembly requirements Mechanical compatibility Automated checks can identify rule violations, but they cannot replace engineering judgment. A professional PCB review therefore combines software-based verification with engineering inspection. Step 6 – Design Review and Customer Approval Before generating final manufacturing data, the completed PCB layout is provided to the customer for review. The customer can verify key aspects of the design, including: Component locations Board dimensions Connector positions Mechanical interfaces Silkscreen information Routing and design intent Any required changes are incorporated before the design is released for manufacturing. This review stage provides an important checkpoint between PCB design and production and helps ensure that the final layout accurately reflects the customer's design requirements. Step 7 – Manufacturing Data Generation Once the PCB layout has been approved, the final manufacturing data is generated. Depending on the project, the manufacturing package may include: Gerber files NC drill files PCB fabrication drawings Bill of Materials (BOM) Pick-and-place files Assembly drawings Stack-up information Other manufacturing documentation Gerber files contain the graphical information required to manufacture the PCB, including copper layers, solder mask, silkscreen, and other fabrication layers. For PCB assembly projects, the BOM and pick-and-place files provide the component and placement information required for SMT assembly. Before release, the output files are checked to ensure that the generated manufacturing data is consistent with the approved PCB design. Step 8 – DFM and PCB Manufacturing The final stage is transferring the verified manufacturing data into production. Before fabrication, the manufacturing data can be evaluated against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities through Design for Manufacturability (DFM) checks. Typical DFM considerations include: Minimum trace width and spacing Minimum drill size Copper-to-edge clearance Annular ring requirements Solder mask clearance Via structures Board thickness Copper thickness Surface finish Manufacturing tolerances Manufacturing requirements are considered from the very beginning of PCBWay's PCB layout process, helping minimize production issues and unnecessary manufacturing delays. What’s more, upon completion of the PCB Layout order, free technical support and a permanent 5% discount on PCBA production will be provided. Why Professional PCB Layout Matters PCB layout has a direct impact on the performance and manufacturability of an electronic product. A professional PCB layout should consider the entire product development process—not just whether all components are electrically connected. Depending on the application, the layout may need to address: Signal Integrity (SI) Power Integrity (PI) EMI/EMC Thermal Management High-Speed Design Design for Manufacturability (DFM) Design for Assembly (DFA) Mechanical Integration Reliability and Serviceability The earlier these factors are considered, the fewer problems are likely to appear during prototype validation and mass production. At PCBWay, our PCB design engineers work with customers throughout the layout process, helping transform circuit concepts and schematics into manufacturable, reliable, and production-ready PCB designs. If you are looking for professional PCB layout or PCB design services, feel free to contact us or submit PCB Layout requirement here. Our engineering team can help evaluate your design and develop a PCB layout optimized for both performance and manufacturing. Verify Now Blog > Power Supply Design and Layout Guidelines for LDO and DCDC Power Supply Design and Layout Guidelines for LDO and DCDC by: Mila Sep 29,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout power supply design DCDC PCB layout power supply layout LDO layout guidelines Power supply design is not simply about choosing the right regulator and adding enough copper. The PCB layout directly affects thermal performance, noise, EMI, stability, and overall power integrity. LDOs and DCDC converters have different layout priorities: LDOs require careful attention to heat dissipation, capacitor placement, and power loss, while DCDC converters are more sensitive to high-frequency current loops, feedback routing, and grounding. When both are used in the same system, power-stage isolation and decoupling become equally important. In this guide, we’ll break down the key power supply layout considerations and common mistakes for LDOs, DCDC converters, and mixed power architectures. 1. LDO (Low-Dropout Regulator): Quiet but Sensitive to Heat （LDO regulator） Advantages: Low noise, no switching interference, and simple peripheral circuitry Disadvantages: Efficiency depends on the input-to-output voltage difference, and large voltage drops or high load currents can generate significant heat. Three Common LDO PCB Layout Mistakes Mistake 1: Poor Thermal Management → Excessive Temperature Rise Incorrect: Leaving the exposed pad floating without sufficient copper area or thermal vias. Consequence: Higher thermal resistance can increase junction temperature, potentially triggering thermal protection or affecting long-term reliability. Correct: Connect the exposed pad to a sufficiently large copper area. Add thermal vias according to the package and datasheet recommendations, connecting them to internal or bottom-layer copper planes. Avoid routing signal traces underneath the thermal pad. Evaluate the required copper area and thermal performance based on actual power dissipation. Mistake 2: Input/Output Capacitors Too Far from the Pins → Reduced Stability and Transient Performance Incorrect: Placing the input and output capacitors far away from the LDO pins. Consequence: Increased parasitic impedance can affect stability, transient response, and high-frequency noise performance. Correct: Place Cin and Cout as close as possible to the corresponding LDO pins. Select capacitor values, quantities, and ESR according to the device datasheet. Prefer low-ESR capacitors recommended by the manufacturer. Keep the feedback path short and avoid unnecessary routing and noise coupling. Mistake 3: Ignoring Voltage Drop and Power Dissipation → Efficiency and Thermal Issues Incorrect: Using an LDO for high input voltage and high current without evaluating power dissipation. Consequence: Higher LDO power dissipation increases junction temperature and may trigger thermal protection or reduce system reliability. Correct: The main power dissipation of an LDO can be estimated using: P ≈ (Vin − Vout) × Iout The larger the voltage drop and output current, the higher the LDO power dissipation. For high-power applications, evaluate efficiency, junction temperature, and PCB thermal performance together. When the voltage drop or load current is high, consider using a DCDC converter first and an LDO for downstream regulation and noise reduction. 2. DCDC (Switching Power Supply): Efficient but Noisy （dc-dc converter） Advantages: High conversion efficiency, higher output current capability, and suitability for a wide range of input and output voltages Disadvantages: Switching nodes and high di/dt currents can generate noise, making DCDC PCB layout critical to EMI, stability, and overall power performance. Five Common DCDC PCB Layout Mistakes Mistake 1: Long Power Loops → Increased Ringing and EMI Incorrect: Placing the input capacitor, power switch, inductor, and other key components too far apart, resulting in a large high-frequency current loop. Consequence: Increased parasitic inductance can produce more pronounced voltage spikes and ringing under high di/dt conditions, increasing EMI and component stress. Correct: Minimize the area of critical high-frequency power loops. Place input bypass capacitors, power devices, and inductors as close together as possible. Use sufficiently wide power traces. The required width should be determined by current, copper thickness, and allowable temperature rise. Avoid unnecessarily long high di/dt return paths. Mistake 2: Noisy Feedback Path → Output Voltage Fluctuation Incorrect: Routing the FB trace close to or parallel with the SW node, inductor, or other noisy areas. Consequence: Switching noise can couple into the feedback network, affecting output voltage regulation and system stability. Correct: Keep the FB trace short and away from the SW node and high di/dt current paths. Place the feedback resistors close to the IC's FB pin. Sense the output voltage from a stable, low-noise point. For high-precision applications, consider Kelvin sensing or other methods recommended by the device manufacturer to reduce voltage drop and noise. Mistake 3: Improper Ground Plane Design → Increased EMI and Noise Incorrect: Improper AGND, PGND, or high-current return-path routing causes sensitive control circuitry to share impedance with power return currents. Consequence: Ground bounce and common-impedance coupling can affect control signals, feedback, and output voltage. Correct: Follow the DCDC IC manufacturer's recommended method for connecting AGND and PGND. Provide a low-impedance return path for PGND. Keep sensitive analog ground areas away from high-current power return paths whenever possible. Prevent high di/dt currents from passing through sensitive signal areas. Mistake 4: Improper Input Capacitor Placement → Increased Input Ripple Incorrect: Relying on a single bulk capacitor while placing it far from the VIN and GND pins. Consequence: A larger high-frequency current loop can increase input ripple and noise. Correct: Configure input capacitors according to the DCDC converter datasheet. Use capacitors with different values when necessary to address different frequency ranges. Place input capacitors as close as possible to the VIN and GND pins. Keep the input capacitor loop short and compact. Mistake 5: Ignoring the Freewheeling Path → Reduced Efficiency and Poorer EMI Performance Incorrect: Placing the freewheeling diode, synchronous MOSFET, or related circuitry too far apart. Consequence: Increased parasitic parameters can lead to additional losses, ringing, and EMI. Correct: Optimize the freewheeling and synchronous rectification paths according to the specific converter topology. Minimize high-current return paths. For multiphase DCDC converters, keep the power paths of each phase well organized and reasonably symmetrical. 3. LDO + DCDC Mixed Power Supply: Balancing Efficiency and Low Noise （power supply pcb） In practical systems, DCDC converters and LDOs are often used together rather than as alternatives. For example: DCDC: 12V → 3.3V for efficient voltage conversion LDO: 3.3V → 1.8V for noise-sensitive circuits such as ADCs, PLLs, and clocks This approach combines the efficiency of a DCDC converter with the low-noise characteristics of an LDO, making it useful for applications that require both power efficiency and clean power rails. Three Common Mixed Power Supply Layout Mistakes Mistake 1: Insufficient Filtering at the LDO Input → Upstream Noise May Reach the Downstream Rail Incorrect: Connecting the DCDC output directly to an LDO-powered sensitive load without evaluating the DCDC switching noise and the LDO's PSRR. Consequence: Switching ripple from the upstream converter may couple into downstream sensitive circuits through the power path, affecting ADC, PLL, and other noise-sensitive devices. Correct: Evaluate whether additional filtering is required based on the DCDC switching frequency, LDO PSRR, and load noise requirements. When necessary, add a ferrite bead, LC filter, or π filter between the two power stages. Place filtering components close to the corresponding power input and keep the filter loop area under control. Avoid adding filtering components blindly; select them based on the actual noise frequency range. Mistake 2: Poor Power Region Layout → Noise Coupling Incorrect: Placing the high-noise DCDC switching area too close to sensitive LDO power areas or creating unnecessary coupling between different power regions. Consequence: Switching noise can couple into sensitive power rails through parasitic capacitance, electromagnetic coupling, or shared impedance. Correct: Properly separate the DCDC power stage, LDO area, and sensitive load areas. Keep high-noise SW nodes away from sensitive power rails and signals. Maintain a solid reference ground plane beneath the LDO output power area whenever possible. Keep sensitive power traces away from high di/dt return paths of the DCDC converter. Mistake 3: Poorly Designed Decoupling Network → Insufficient High-Frequency Response Incorrect: Placing all capacitors at the DCDC output while providing insufficient local decoupling near sensitive loads. Consequence: Parasitic impedance in the power path can reduce high-frequency decoupling effectiveness, preventing the load from receiving transient current quickly enough. Correct: Configure DCDC output capacitors according to the converter requirements. Use the required input and output capacitors at the LDO according to the datasheet. Add local decoupling capacitors close to sensitive loads such as ADCs, PLLs, and MCUs. Design each power stage's decoupling network according to the actual load and frequency requirements rather than simply adding more capacitors. Conclusion Although LDOs and DCDC converters are both power management devices, their power supply layout priorities are different. LDO layout guidelines focus more on thermal management, capacitor placement, and power dissipation. DCDC PCB layout focuses more on high-frequency power loops, feedback paths, grounding, and EMI. Mixed power supplies require additional attention to noise isolation and decoupling between different power stages. A good power supply pcb design is not simply about adding more copper. It is about giving current the shortest and most appropriate path, keeping noise away from sensitive areas, and placing every critical component where it can perform properly. Verify Now Blog > Why Antipads Matter for Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design Why Antipads Matter for Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design by: Mila Sep 21,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout signal integrity PCB antipad high-speed PCB design anti pad pcb In high-speed PCB design , via antipads are often treated as simple clearance features. In fact, the size of a PCB antipad directly affects the parasitic capacitance and local impedance around a via, making it an important parameter for maintaining impedance continuity and signal integrity. If the antipad is too small, it can introduce excessive capacitive loading and cause local impedance to drop. If it is too large, it may affect the integrity of the power or ground plane. Especially in Gbps-level high-speed links, simply using the default parameters in PCB design software can result in significant impedance discontinuities around the via transition, potentially affecting signal integrity. The purpose of an anti pad PCB design is not limited to preventing electrical shorts. By changing the electromagnetic coupling between the via and reference plane, a properly designed antipad can reduce via parasitic capacitance, optimize local impedance, and minimize signal reflections. Therefore, antipad design is an important part of optimizing high-speed vias. What Is a PCB Antipad Actually “Removing”? Let's put aside the abstract definition and look at it from a straightforward engineering perspective. When a PCB via changes layers, its metal barrel and pad pass through portions of the power and ground planes. The metal conductor, dielectric material, and surrounding plane copper naturally form parasitic capacitance. The impedance of a transmission line is mainly determined by the dielectric material, trace width, and stackup. However, the additional parasitic capacitance around a via introduces extra capacitive loading, causing the local via impedance to deviate from the target impedance of the transmission line. This creates an impedance discontinuity that can affect high-speed signal transmission. A PCB antipad is a copper clearance area created around the via pad on the power or ground plane layers through which the via passes. Its main purposes are: Increase the distance between the via barrel and plane copper to prevent electrical shorts; Reduce the parasitic capacitance between the via and reference plane, optimize local via impedance, and reduce reflections caused by impedance discontinuity. A high-speed signal trace can be compared to a smooth road with a constant speed limit. The via is an unavoidable intersection, while parasitic capacitance is like a sudden dip in the road. When the signal travels through this discontinuity at high speed, impedance changes can cause reflections, ringing, and waveform distortion. The purpose of an antipad is to adjust the electromagnetic coupling between the via and reference plane, reducing the impact of this “dip” and making the via transition smoother. （Anti-pad Structure） How Does Parasitic Capacitance Affect Via Impedance? A via is not an ideal conductor. Its equivalent model can include parasitic inductance L and parasitic capacitance C. For high-speed signals, the actual impedance characteristics of a via are also affected by factors such as via length, hole diameter, pad size, antipad size, reference plane position, and via stub. The antipad size is one of the important parameters affecting via parasitic capacitance. If the antipad is too small, the distance between the via barrel or pad and the reference plane becomes smaller, increasing the capacitive loading between the via and plane. This can cause a more significant drop in local via impedance. For example, when a transmission line with a target impedance of 50 Ω passes through an unoptimized via structure, the local impedance may decrease around the via transition, creating a structure such as: 50 Ω trace → lower impedance at via → 50 Ω trace. This impedance discontinuity can cause signal reflections, energy loss, and waveform distortion. Therefore, an antipad is not simply a matter of making the clearance as large or as small as possible. In high-speed PCB design, its size needs to be optimized together with the stackup, via structure, and target impedance. （Small antipad vs Large antipad） What Problems Can Improper Antipad Design Cause? It is easy to assume that a small dimensional difference will not matter. However, in Gbps-level high-speed links, even small geometric changes in the via structure can affect impedance and signal integrity. 1. Impedance Discontinuity, Signal Reflection, and Reduced Eye Opening A smaller antipad → higher parasitic capacitance → potentially lower local via impedance. When a high-speed signal reaches this region, a significant impedance change can cause signal reflection, edge distortion, increased jitter, and reduced eye opening. These effects may ultimately degrade the performance of the high-speed link. 2. Poorer Return Loss and Reflected Signal Energy Impedance discontinuities increase signal reflection, causing part of the signal energy to return toward the transmitter instead of reaching the receiver effectively. For high-speed SerDes links, reflections from multiple vias, connectors, and package structures can accumulate. Therefore, maintaining impedance continuity across the via transition is an important part of signal integrity optimization. 3. Via Resonance and Stub Effects Can Increase Loss at Specific Frequencies The parasitic inductance and capacitance of a via, together with unused via stubs, can create frequency-dependent resonance and reflection characteristics. When the effective frequency range of a high-speed signal approaches these resonant regions, return loss and insertion loss may deteriorate significantly. This is one reason why some links may work normally at lower speeds but show degraded performance at higher data rates. Therefore, in addition to PCB antipad design, high-speed via design also needs to consider via stubs. For loss-sensitive high-speed links, techniques such as back drilling, blind vias, or buried vias can be used to shorten or eliminate unnecessary via stubs. 4. Reference Plane Discontinuity and Poorer Return Current Paths An antipad should not simply be made as large as possible. If the plane clearance becomes excessively large, it may affect the continuity of the local reference plane and force the high-speed return current to take a longer path. This can increase return-path inductance and introduce additional impedance discontinuities. In high-density high-speed PCB design, the locations of adjacent vias, return vias, and reference planes should also be considered together to avoid creating new signal integrity or EMI problems through excessive plane clearance. Not Just Vias: BGA Areas Also Need Attention Most high-speed PCB designs focus heavily on via antipads, but in high-density BGA regions, the parasitic capacitance between component pads and reference planes also deserves attention. A typical high-speed trace may be only 3–4 mil wide, while a BGA pad is usually much larger than the trace. The larger the pad area and the closer it is to the reference plane, the greater the potential capacitive loading. A large pad located close to a reference plane can introduce additional capacitive loading, making the BGA breakout region another potential impedance transition in a high-speed signal path. Therefore, high-speed BGA design should consider: BGA pad size; Distance between the pad and reference plane; Trace width and impedance; Breakout method; Reference plane continuity. When necessary, local plane clearance can be used to reduce the parasitic capacitance associated with the pad. However, not every BGA pad requires an enlarged antipad. Excessive plane clearance can also disrupt reference plane continuity and force the return current to detour. Therefore, the appropriate clearance should be determined based on the stackup, pad geometry, target impedance, and simulation results. How Should a Differential Via Antipad Be Designed? A single-ended signal via can typically use a circular antipad, but differential vias should not simply follow the same design approach. 1. Separate Circular Antipads May Introduce Additional Coupling If the positive and negative differential vias each use an independent circular antipad, a narrow strip of reference plane copper may remain between the two antipads. This remaining copper can change the electromagnetic coupling between the two vias. For high-speed differential signals, such a structural change may affect: Differential impedance Symmetry between the two signal paths Differential-to-common-mode conversion Insertion loss and return loss around the via transition 2. Connected Oval or “Dog-Bone” Antipad When space allows and simulation confirms the design, the antipads around the two differential vias can be partially connected to form an oval or “dog-bone” clearance area. This approach can reduce unnecessary plane copper between the two vias and create a more symmetrical electromagnetic environment around the differential via pair. The main benefits include: Better control of differential impedance toward the target value; Improved structural symmetry and reduced risk of differential-to-common-mode conversion; Reduced unnecessary local electromagnetic coupling between the vias. However, a dog-bone-shaped antipad is not a universal solution for every differential via structure. The final shape and dimensions should still be determined based on via spacing, stackup, target impedance, and simulation results. How Large Should a PCB Antipad Be? Antipad design is a typical case of “too much of a good thing.” If the antipad is too small, electromagnetic coupling between the via and reference plane increases, potentially increasing parasitic capacitance. If it is too large, reference plane continuity may be affected. Therefore, the PCB antipad needs to balance impedance control, return current paths, and manufacturing capability. Key Guidelines for High-Speed PCB Antipad Design 1. Do Not Simply Apply a Fixed Mil Value There is no universal antipad size that works for every high-speed PCB. The actual dimensions should be optimized according to via hole diameter, pad size, dielectric thickness, material Dk, reference plane position, and target impedance. 2. Meet Manufacturing Rules Before Optimizing Impedance An initial antipad size can be established according to the PCB manufacturer's design rules and then refined through impedance calculation or simulation. 3. Maintain Symmetry in Differential Vias For differential via structures, the geometry and electromagnetic environment around the positive and negative vias should be as symmetrical as possible to maintain differential impedance and reduce mode conversion. 4. Simulate the Complete Via Transition for High-Speed Links For high-speed links above 10 Gbps, as well as interfaces such as PCIe, USB, and SerDes that have strict requirements for channel loss and impedance continuity, fixed empirical dimensions should not be applied directly. The complete stackup, material Dk/Df, via geometry, reference planes, return vias, and target impedance should be considered together. For complex three-dimensional via structures, tools such as HFSS, CST, or Simbeor can be used for electromagnetic analysis, while tools such as Polar SI9000 are more suitable for PCB stackup and transmission-line impedance analysis. The acceptable impedance variation should ultimately be determined according to the specific interface specification and channel budget rather than applying a single universal ±10% requirement. Conclusion Effective high-speed PCB design is not simply about creating an antipad around a via. It requires an understanding of the relationship between parasitic capacitance, via impedance, reference planes, return current paths, and signal integrity. An antipad that is too small may increase capacitive loading and cause local impedance to decrease, while an oversized antipad may affect reference plane continuity. For high-speed differential vias, designers must also consider structural symmetry, differential impedance, and mode conversion. Therefore, there is no single antipad size that is suitable for every PCB. A properly designed PCB antipad should be optimized according to the target impedance and signal integrity requirements, together with the PCB stackup, via geometry, manufacturing capability, and simulation results. This helps maintain a more continuous and stable electromagnetic environment throughout the high-speed signal path. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Why Antipads Matter for Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design Why Antipads Matter for Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design by: Mila Sep 21,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout signal integrity PCB antipad high-speed PCB design anti pad pcb In high-speed PCB design , via antipads are often treated as simple clearance features. In fact, the size of a PCB antipad directly affects the parasitic capacitance and local impedance around a via, making it an important parameter for maintaining impedance continuity and signal integrity. If the antipad is too small, it can introduce excessive capacitive loading and cause local impedance to drop. If it is too large, it may affect the integrity of the power or ground plane. Especially in Gbps-level high-speed links, simply using the default parameters in PCB design software can result in significant impedance discontinuities around the via transition, potentially affecting signal integrity. The purpose of an anti pad PCB design is not limited to preventing electrical shorts. By changing the electromagnetic coupling between the via and reference plane, a properly designed antipad can reduce via parasitic capacitance, optimize local impedance, and minimize signal reflections. Therefore, antipad design is an important part of optimizing high-speed vias. What Is a PCB Antipad Actually “Removing”? Let's put aside the abstract definition and look at it from a straightforward engineering perspective. When a PCB via changes layers, its metal barrel and pad pass through portions of the power and ground planes. The metal conductor, dielectric material, and surrounding plane copper naturally form parasitic capacitance. The impedance of a transmission line is mainly determined by the dielectric material, trace width, and stackup. However, the additional parasitic capacitance around a via introduces extra capacitive loading, causing the local via impedance to deviate from the target impedance of the transmission line. This creates an impedance discontinuity that can affect high-speed signal transmission. A PCB antipad is a copper clearance area created around the via pad on the power or ground plane layers through which the via passes. Its main purposes are: Increase the distance between the via barrel and plane copper to prevent electrical shorts; Reduce the parasitic capacitance between the via and reference plane, optimize local via impedance, and reduce reflections caused by impedance discontinuity. A high-speed signal trace can be compared to a smooth road with a constant speed limit. The via is an unavoidable intersection, while parasitic capacitance is like a sudden dip in the road. When the signal travels through this discontinuity at high speed, impedance changes can cause reflections, ringing, and waveform distortion. The purpose of an antipad is to adjust the electromagnetic coupling between the via and reference plane, reducing the impact of this “dip” and making the via transition smoother. （Anti-pad Structure） How Does Parasitic Capacitance Affect Via Impedance? A via is not an ideal conductor. Its equivalent model can include parasitic inductance L and parasitic capacitance C. For high-speed signals, the actual impedance characteristics of a via are also affected by factors such as via length, hole diameter, pad size, antipad size, reference plane position, and via stub. The antipad size is one of the important parameters affecting via parasitic capacitance. If the antipad is too small, the distance between the via barrel or pad and the reference plane becomes smaller, increasing the capacitive loading between the via and plane. This can cause a more significant drop in local via impedance. For example, when a transmission line with a target impedance of 50 Ω passes through an unoptimized via structure, the local impedance may decrease around the via transition, creating a structure such as: 50 Ω trace → lower impedance at via → 50 Ω trace. This impedance discontinuity can cause signal reflections, energy loss, and waveform distortion. Therefore, an antipad is not simply a matter of making the clearance as large or as small as possible. In high-speed PCB design, its size needs to be optimized together with the stackup, via structure, and target impedance. （Small antipad vs Large antipad） What Problems Can Improper Antipad Design Cause? It is easy to assume that a small dimensional difference will not matter. However, in Gbps-level high-speed links, even small geometric changes in the via structure can affect impedance and signal integrity. 1. Impedance Discontinuity, Signal Reflection, and Reduced Eye Opening A smaller antipad → higher parasitic capacitance → potentially lower local via impedance. When a high-speed signal reaches this region, a significant impedance change can cause signal reflection, edge distortion, increased jitter, and reduced eye opening. These effects may ultimately degrade the performance of the high-speed link. 2. Poorer Return Loss and Reflected Signal Energy Impedance discontinuities increase signal reflection, causing part of the signal energy to return toward the transmitter instead of reaching the receiver effectively. For high-speed SerDes links, reflections from multiple vias, connectors, and package structures can accumulate. Therefore, maintaining impedance continuity across the via transition is an important part of signal integrity optimization. 3. Via Resonance and Stub Effects Can Increase Loss at Specific Frequencies The parasitic inductance and capacitance of a via, together with unused via stubs, can create frequency-dependent resonance and reflection characteristics. When the effective frequency range of a high-speed signal approaches these resonant regions, return loss and insertion loss may deteriorate significantly. This is one reason why some links may work normally at lower speeds but show degraded performance at higher data rates. Therefore, in addition to PCB antipad design, high-speed via design also needs to consider via stubs. For loss-sensitive high-speed links, techniques such as back drilling, blind vias, or buried vias can be used to shorten or eliminate unnecessary via stubs. 4. Reference Plane Discontinuity and Poorer Return Current Paths An antipad should not simply be made as large as possible. If the plane clearance becomes excessively large, it may affect the continuity of the local reference plane and force the high-speed return current to take a longer path. This can increase return-path inductance and introduce additional impedance discontinuities. In high-density high-speed PCB design, the locations of adjacent vias, return vias, and reference planes should also be considered together to avoid creating new signal integrity or EMI problems through excessive plane clearance. Not Just Vias: BGA Areas Also Need Attention Most high-speed PCB designs focus heavily on via antipads, but in high-density BGA regions, the parasitic capacitance between component pads and reference planes also deserves attention. A typical high-speed trace may be only 3–4 mil wide, while a BGA pad is usually much larger than the trace. The larger the pad area and the closer it is to the reference plane, the greater the potential capacitive loading. A large pad located close to a reference plane can introduce additional capacitive loading, making the BGA breakout region another potential impedance transition in a high-speed signal path. Therefore, high-speed BGA design should consider: BGA pad size; Distance between the pad and reference plane; Trace width and impedance; Breakout method; Reference plane continuity. When necessary, local plane clearance can be used to reduce the parasitic capacitance associated with the pad. However, not every BGA pad requires an enlarged antipad. Excessive plane clearance can also disrupt reference plane continuity and force the return current to detour. Therefore, the appropriate clearance should be determined based on the stackup, pad geometry, target impedance, and simulation results. How Should a Differential Via Antipad Be Designed? A single-ended signal via can typically use a circular antipad, but differential vias should not simply follow the same design approach. 1. Separate Circular Antipads May Introduce Additional Coupling If the positive and negative differential vias each use an independent circular antipad, a narrow strip of reference plane copper may remain between the two antipads. This remaining copper can change the electromagnetic coupling between the two vias. For high-speed differential signals, such a structural change may affect: Differential impedance Symmetry between the two signal paths Differential-to-common-mode conversion Insertion loss and return loss around the via transition 2. Connected Oval or “Dog-Bone” Antipad When space allows and simulation confirms the design, the antipads around the two differential vias can be partially connected to form an oval or “dog-bone” clearance area. This approach can reduce unnecessary plane copper between the two vias and create a more symmetrical electromagnetic environment around the differential via pair. The main benefits include: Better control of differential impedance toward the target value; Improved structural symmetry and reduced risk of differential-to-common-mode conversion; Reduced unnecessary local electromagnetic coupling between the vias. However, a dog-bone-shaped antipad is not a universal solution for every differential via structure. The final shape and dimensions should still be determined based on via spacing, stackup, target impedance, and simulation results. How Large Should a PCB Antipad Be? Antipad design is a typical case of “too much of a good thing.” If the antipad is too small, electromagnetic coupling between the via and reference plane increases, potentially increasing parasitic capacitance. If it is too large, reference plane continuity may be affected. Therefore, the PCB antipad needs to balance impedance control, return current paths, and manufacturing capability. Key Guidelines for High-Speed PCB Antipad Design 1. Do Not Simply Apply a Fixed Mil Value There is no universal antipad size that works for every high-speed PCB. The actual dimensions should be optimized according to via hole diameter, pad size, dielectric thickness, material Dk, reference plane position, and target impedance. 2. Meet Manufacturing Rules Before Optimizing Impedance An initial antipad size can be established according to the PCB manufacturer's design rules and then refined through impedance calculation or simulation. 3. Maintain Symmetry in Differential Vias For differential via structures, the geometry and electromagnetic environment around the positive and negative vias should be as symmetrical as possible to maintain differential impedance and reduce mode conversion. 4. Simulate the Complete Via Transition for High-Speed Links For high-speed links above 10 Gbps, as well as interfaces such as PCIe, USB, and SerDes that have strict requirements for channel loss and impedance continuity, fixed empirical dimensions should not be applied directly. The complete stackup, material Dk/Df, via geometry, reference planes, return vias, and target impedance should be considered together. For complex three-dimensional via structures, tools such as HFSS, CST, or Simbeor can be used for electromagnetic analysis, while tools such as Polar SI9000 are more suitable for PCB stackup and transmission-line impedance analysis. The acceptable impedance variation should ultimately be determined according to the specific interface specification and channel budget rather than applying a single universal ±10% requirement. Conclusion Effective high-speed PCB design is not simply about creating an antipad around a via. It requires an understanding of the relationship between parasitic capacitance, via impedance, reference planes, return current paths, and signal integrity. An antipad that is too small may increase capacitive loading and cause local impedance to decrease, while an oversized antipad may affect reference plane continuity. For high-speed differential vias, designers must also consider structural symmetry, differential impedance, and mode conversion. Therefore, there is no single antipad size that is suitable for every PCB. A properly designed PCB antipad should be optimized according to the target impedance and signal integrity requirements, together with the PCB stackup, via geometry, manufacturing capability, and simulation results. This helps maintain a more continuous and stable electromagnetic environment throughout the high-speed signal path. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac.
